title: Behar: strangers and settlers (Leviticus 25:23)
hook: the land is God's, "for ye are strangers and settlers with Me"

segments.voice: Yesterday the shofar sounded for the fiftieth year, the yovel, and your line was proclaim liberty. Did one old debt, owed to you or by you, get a little lighter? Day four hundred twenty-two.

Somewhere there's a deed with your family's name on it, or a lease, or at least a parking spot you think of as yours. Every culture has a way of saying mine. A fence, a title, a signature at a closing table with too many pens. The Torah's law of the land has paperwork too: fields are bought and sold in Leviticus, with prices worked out by the year. And then, in the middle of all those transactions, God says something that turns every deed into a rental agreement. The field you just paid for was never really for sale.
screen: `A DEED, A LEASE, A FENCE.` → `FIELDS BOUGHT AND SOLD.` → `NEVER REALLY FOR SALE.`

segments.voice: This week's portion is called Behar, on the mountain, because it opens at Sinai. We've already met the rest year and the jubilee, when land goes home to the family that first held it. Here is the reason the Torah gives, in Leviticus twenty-five, verse twenty-three: "And the land shall not be sold in perpetuity; for the land is Mine; for ye are strangers and settlers with Me." In Hebrew, gerim v'toshavim. A ger is a resident outsider, someone living in a place that isn't originally theirs. A toshav is a settler, someone staying on. Put them together and you get a careful picture: you really live here, you plant and harvest and raise children here, and still, you're a guest. Notice the last word: with Me. Not strangers to God, strangers alongside God, sharing the house with its owner. The same phrase runs through the Bible's prayers and stories. Abraham, buying a burial cave for Sarah, introduces himself to the Hittites as a stranger and a sojourner. A psalm asks God to hear, because the singer is a stranger with God, a sojourner, as all their ancestors were. So the law does two things at once. It protects the poor family that had to sell, because the land comes back. And it reminds the wealthy buyer that they hold a lease, not a crown. Commentators down the centuries have read it as a check on pride: if even the land is borrowed, so is almost everything in your hands.
screen: `BEHAR: ON THE MOUNTAIN.` · `THE LAND IS MINE.` · `GERIM V'TOSHAVIM: GUESTS WHO STAY.` · `A LEASE, NOT A CROWN.` · then, large: `STRANGERS AND SETTLERS WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one possession loosely. Pick up something near you that you'd call yours. A phone, a ring, a key. Feel its weight in your hand. Then open your hand flat, so it rests on your palm instead of in your grip. Breathe, and think about where it came from, who made it, how long it will outlast you or how soon it won't. You don't have to give it away. Just hold it the way a guest holds a borrowed cup. The bell holds the time.
Behar. On the mountain: the portion that says the land rests, the land returns, and everyone on it is a guest of its owner.
Your line: we are guests here. Today, treat one shared space, a kitchen, a park, an office, the way a good guest would, and leave it a little better. Day four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Behar is read in synagogue in the spring, often paired with Bechukotai. In the Land of Israel some farmers still let fields rest in the seventh year, and the idea that the earth belongs to God shapes Jewish teaching about property and charity.

fork.setup: you're a wealthy buyer in ancient Israel. you've just paid for a poor family's field. what does the law say you've bought?
options: the harvests until the jubilee year.
nothing at all; the sale is forbidden.
fork.reveal: the price is set by the years left until the jubilee. you bought a lease on the harvests, because the land itself belongs to God.

original.note: Hebrew: strangers and settlers. guests who live here, and still guests.

trapdoor: what you thought: a field you buy is simply yours, forever.
what it means: in Leviticus the land is God's, and the people who farm it live on it as strangers and settlers with God.
what a scholar hears: the price of land in Leviticus 25:15–16 is counted by the harvests left before the jubilee; a sale is really a lease.
